newsitem.title: USA: Boutros-Ghali advocates big step for Mideast talks.
newsitem.headline: Boutros-Ghali advocates big step for Mideast talks.

text.p: Former U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said the Middle East peace process needed a dramatic step to break the deadlock, similar to the 1977 visit to Jerusalem by Egypt's late President Anwar Sadat.

He also said on Tuesday intensive diplomacy was needed at the highest level, small confidence-building steps had to be taken immediately and international public opinion had to be mobilised again in favour of a peace agreement.
"Time is not in favour of the Palestinians in the short term," he said. "Time is a neutral enemy."

He was speaking to reporters at Egypt's U.N. mission to promote the publication of his book on the negotiations leading to the 1979 Camp David peace agreements between Israel and Egypt and ending with the assassination of Sadat in 1981.

The book, "Egypt's Road to Jerusalem," is being issued by Random House this week. In it he details his observations on the peace process from a front row seat as Egypt's secretary of state for foreign affairs and acting foreign minister.
Asked what he would do today to break the two-month deadlock in the peace process, he said the first thing needed was a vision, a dramatic step to jump-start the talks.
"I will say that we need first a great vision, something which might create a shock like the visit to President Sadat to Jerusalem," Boutros-Ghali said.

Then, he said, intensive diplomacy was needed "at the highest level" between Israeli President Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian leader Yassir Arafat. At the same time momentum had to be created through small steps designed to foster confidence, perhaps unification of some families.

"The Palestinians say the Israelis do not respect peace accords. And the Israelis have not been able to have the security they thought would come from the agreements ... there is a crisis of confidence," he said.
It also was important to get the international community, including the American public, interested in the issue again.
"The international community is indifferent. It is not now interested in the Middle East crisis," he said. "Without mobilising public opinion, we will not be able to create a new momentum."
A dramatic gesture might serve this end, but asked what that should be, he said, "I don't know but with a bit of imagination we can find something."
He said the Palestinians would be wise to move on any front possible, noting that opportunities had been missed 25 years ago because "each time we postponed the situation."

He said the late Prime Minister Menachem Begin's position in 1977 was not much different from Netanyahu's stance today. "So there is no reason not to solve the problem today as we had done in 1977," he said.
But he said moderates had to be encouraged by their allies throughout the world because "the fundamentalists, the extremists" opposed to peace accords had been successful.
"The fundamentalists killed Sadat (and) the fundamentalists belonging to the other camp killed Prime Minister (Yitzhak) Rabin" in 1995.

Boutros-Ghali was U.N. secretary-general for five years, ending in 1996 when Washington vetoed his re-election bid for allegedly not moving quickly on reform. An international law professor by training, he has written several books and is working on another one about his years in the world body.
